reasoning: ح is 7 and the shadda doubles it. The verb is ka77, and 3indi ku77a is how you say you have a cough.
ق is a glottal stop and the shadda doubles the f; taa marbuta after ف is e. A woven or plastic produce basket; plural 'ufaf.
One syllable, no case ending. Collective, used for beach and building sand alike.
The word-initial madda is a vowel seat, so only the long aa is written. Borrowed telephone greeting, used exactly as in the English allo.

meaning_fix: as if you hadn't said anything / you might as well not have spoken
reasoning: ka'annak contracts to kaannak, matching the headword spelling. It says the words had no effect, which is not quite the same as advising silence.
The final hamza is dropped in speech, so the Arabic is respelt دُعَا. Personal supplication, as distinct from the ritual Salaa.
illi is the relative pronoun and the b-imperfect carries the general-truth sense. The shadda doubles the b of 7ibb in both verbs.
ص is emphatic S. The past khiliS is the it-finished form, not the interjection khalaS; 3ala plus the first-person suffix doubles the y.
fi3il pattern with two short i vowels. Said of someone getting away and of something slipping loose from your hand.
ظ is the emphatic interdental, written TH. Politically or socially conservative; the identical word is also the title of a district governor.
Shadda doubles the y. Both senses are live in Ramallah, and il-hawiyye on its own is the ID card everyone carries.
kaan plus the b-imperfect is the habitual past. barra has a shadda on the r; the headword's final و is the plural ending.
Form III verbal noun used as the sport's name; taa marbuta after م is e. A sports-page word rather than a street one, but it is what people say.
The headword spelling أروبا is missing the واو: the name is أوروبا, said oorubba with a long oo and a doubled b. The vowelling gives the name as it is actually pronounced.
Form II with the shadda doubling the l. sallam 3ala is to greet; the same verb also means to hand something over.
The English word group, borrowed for a WhatsApp group, with غ standing in for the loan sound g. Spelt identically to ghuruub 'sunset', so the vowelling matters here.
Form II with ق as a glottal stop and the shadda doubling the f. ش is a sun letter, so bish-shughl.
Long ee, not the MSA diphthong ghayr. Also used as a negator before adjectives, gheer mumkin.

The English says to a woman, so the verb is second-person feminine with -ni, wa7ashtiini, and the Arabic is respelt with ي. The pattern is Egyptian in flavour and widely used, but a Ramallah speaker's own phrase is ishta'tillik.
ث in thaani is said t, so the Arabic is respelt تَانِي. ya3ni is the all-purpose Palestinian filler that opens the rephrasing.
From French service; the shared yellow taxi or minibus that runs a fixed route, central to getting around Ramallah. Many speakers say it with a plain f rather than the loan v.

meaning_fix: popped / burst / banged; in slang also took off, went
reasoning: Geminate verb: ط is emphatic T and the shadda doubles the glottal ق. The basic sense is a pop or a knock, with the going-off sense an extension of it.
The short vowel of the first syllable drops, as in kbiir and jdiid. The upper forehead; the whole brow area is also called jabha.
Both ق glottalise in ordinary speech about police or press investigations, though in formal broadcast style it is read ta7qiiq.
English loan, word-initial hamza on a vowel seat. The Arabic is3aaf is at least as common in Ramallah.
